I've been working this land for 40 years and I know what Quzhou's climate and soils demand. My 7 mu runs the full wheat-maize rotation — winter wheat goes in after maize harvest in October, summer maize goes in right after wheat harvest in June. Every mu works twice a year.

With some family members earning off-farm income, I'm not squeezed for cash, so I won't cut corners on inputs. I've seen too many neighbors chase short-term savings and lose yield. With my education I've kept up with the county agricultural extension recommendations, but I temper them with four decades of watching how my specific fields respond.

**On wheat:** I'll rotary-till after maize straw chopping — the residue needs to be incorporated properly or my seedbed is a mess. I'll go with an improved variety like Kenong 199, which handles our frost and disease pressure well. I split my nitrogen — basal before sowing, then top-dress at jointing. I irrigate four times: sowing water to establish the stand, freeze water in November to protect roots, jointing, and flowering. Powdery mildew and aphids are my main threats, so two pesticide passes.

**On maize:** I direct-seed into the wheat stubble with no tillage — it saves time at the busiest point of the year when the turnaround between harvest and planting is only a few days. I'll use a commercial hybrid, probably Xianyu 335 or similar proven for this area. Summer rains help, but I'll irrigate at planting if soil is dry, again at tasseling, and at grain filling if August turns dry. Two pesticide applications: a herbicide pass early, and one for corn borer if trapping shows pressure.

I'm not chasing record yields — I want stable, profitable yields that don't exhaust my soil or my well.

Summer maize is direct-seeded no-till into wheat stubble to compress the turnaround window, planted with a proven commercial hybrid at 18 kg N/mu to support high grain demand, with three irrigations timed to planting, tasseling, and grain fill.
